title: Industrial Bank – accumulated-impairment reconciliation
source: Exercise Impairment.pdf (course readings, Lecture 3) + worked solution
problem:
On the **balance sheet** of the Industrial Bank, you read the following:

| Loans to customers | 2021 | 2020 | 2019 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|  | 16,250,000 | (not shown) | 16,000,000 |

From the **notes** to the annual accounts:

• Accumulated impairments at the end of 2019 were **450,000**.
• In 2020 the accumulated impairments increased by **100,000** and the bank extended new loans of **525,000**.

Answer the four sub-questions below.
keyFormulas: Gross loans = Net loans (BS) + Accumulated impairment
Acc. impairment (end) = Acc. impairment (begin) + new impairments − write-offs

parts.prompt: Q1 – What is the **gross** loans-to-customers figure at the end of 2019?
working: The balance sheet shows **net** loans (after impairment provisions).

parts.prompt: Q2 – What is the figure for loans to customers at the end of 2020 that will be exhibited on the balance sheet (net)?
Q3 – In 2019 the bank wrote off loans with accumulated impairments of 10,000 and recognised new impairments of 75,000. What were the accumulated impairments at the **beginning** of 2019?
Q4 – In 2021 no new loans were extended and no loans were written off. What were the accumulated impairments at the end of 2021, and what was the impairment expense in P&L for 2021?
working: Strict-consistency reading (continuing from Q2's gross of 16,975,000):
**Textbook solution (the published answer key uses Gross 2021 = 16,450,000, implying the 2020 new loans of 525,000 were offset by 525,000 of write-offs):**

intuition: Q4's published answer (750,000 / 200,000) silently assumes 525,000 of fully-impairment-covered loans were also written off in 2020 – otherwise it contradicts Q2. On an exam, write out the gross-loan roll-forward explicitly so the marker can follow your assumption. The mechanics are the same either way: accumulated impairment moves only via new charges and write-offs; gross loans move only via originations, repayments and write-offs.

title: IFRS 9 three-loan portfolio: ECL across stage transitions
source: May 2025 Final, Q4a + Q4b
problem:
A bank holds three loans. PD₁₂ₘ = 12-month probability of default; PD = lifetime probability of default; LGD = loss given default; EAD = exposure at default.

| Loan | Year 1 | Year 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Stage 1; EAD 100; PD₁₂ₘ 1%; PDₗᵢfₑ 8%; LGD 10% | Stage 3; EAD 100; LGD 10% |
| **2** | Stage 2; EAD 50; PDₗᵢfₑ 20%; LGD 50% | Paid back in full (EAD 0) |
| **3** | Stage 1; EAD 75; PD₁₂ₘ 2%; PDₗᵢfₑ 10%; LGD 20% | Stage 1; EAD 75; PD₁₂ₘ 2%; PDₗᵢfₑ 8%; LGD 20% |

Compute (i) the total **book value** of these loans on the balance sheet at the end of years 1 and 2 with calculations, and (ii) the **total impact on impairment cost in P&L for year 2**.
keyFormulas: Stage 1 → 12-month ECL = EAD × PD₁₂ₘ × LGD
Stage 2 → Lifetime ECL = EAD × PDₗᵢfₑ × LGD
Stage 3 → Default = EAD × 100% × LGD
Book value = EAD − ECL provision
P&L impairment expense (year t) = Acc. ECL (end t) − Acc. ECL (end t−1)

parts.prompt: Year 2 – net impairment expense in P&L.
working: P&L expense Year 2 = Acc. ECL Y2 − Acc. ECL Y1 = 10.30 − 5.40 = **4.90 (expense)**.
Decomposition: Loan 2 paid back → 5.00 reversal (credit). Loan 1 deteriorated to S3 → 9.90 new charge (debit). Loan 3 unchanged → 0. Net 9.90 − 5.00 = **4.90**.

intuition: Stage 1 uses 12-month ECL; Stage 2 jumps to **lifetime** ECL (the big step in absolute amount); Stage 3 treats default as certain so PD = 100%. When a loan is repaid, its prior provision is fully reversed through P&L.

title: Gross loans from net + accumulated impairment
source: Feb 2024 Mid-term, Q4
problem: At year-end 2023 a bank reports **net loans** of 10,000 on the balance sheet and discloses **accumulated impairment** on those loans of 80 in the notes. What were the **gross loans** at the end of 2023?
keyFormulas: Gross loans = Net loans (BS) + Accumulated impairment
intuition: The balance sheet shows loans **after** subtracting cumulative provisions for expected credit losses. Adding back gives the bank's gross exposure to its borrowers.

title: Impairment reconciliation: solving for written-off loans
source: Feb 2024 Mid-term, Q5
problem:
A bank reports:

| Item | Value |
|---|---:|
| Accumulated impairment, year-end 2022 | 100 |
| Accumulated impairment, year-end 2023 | 80 |
| New impairment recognised in P&L 2023 (relating to loans still on the BS at year-end 2023) | 10 |
| Average accumulated-impairment provision on loans derecognised / written off in 2023 | 20% |

What was the **total of the loans on a gross basis written off in 2023**?
keyFormulas: Acc. impairment (end) = Acc. impairment (begin) + new charge − impairment removed via write-off
Impairment removed via write-off = Gross loan written off × coverage ratio

parts.prompt: Step 1 – solve for the impairment removed via write-off (call it X).
working: So 30 of accumulated impairment was released when loans were written off in 2023.

parts.prompt: Step 2 – back out the gross loans written off.
working: The 30 of impairment represented 20% of the gross written-off amount.

intuition: Three movements affect accumulated impairment: (i) new P&L charges (additions), (ii) reversals (subtractions), (iii) write-offs (subtractions, at the coverage ratio). Knowing the opening and closing balance and any two of those movements lets you solve for the third.

title: ECL change on a Stage 1 → Stage 2 downgrade
source: Custom drill in the IFRS 9 framework
problem:
A bank originates a **5,000,000** loan to a retail SME. At inception (Stage 1): PD₁₂ₘ = **0.5%**, LGD = **25%**. After six months a covenant breach signals a significant increase in credit risk and the loan is moved to Stage 2: PDₗᵢfₑ = **4%**, LGD unchanged at 25%. EAD is unchanged.

Compute (i) the impairment booked at inception, (ii) the impairment after the downgrade, and (iii) the increase recognised in P&L when the downgrade is booked.
keyFormulas: Stage 1 ECL = EAD × PD₁₂ₘ × LGD
Stage 2 ECL = EAD × PDₗᵢfₑ × LGD

parts.prompt: P&L impairment expense at the moment of downgrade.

intuition: The Stage 1 → Stage 2 jump is mechanical: PD switches from a 12-month measurement window to a lifetime measurement window. Even with no change in LGD or EAD, the multiplier expansion (here 8×) drives most of the increase in provisions.

title: Stage 1 → Stage 3 default with collateral revaluation
source: Custom drill in the IFRS 9 framework
problem:
A loan with EAD = **1,000,000** is in Stage 1 with PD₁₂ₘ = **1.5%** and LGD = **30%**. The borrower defaults and the loan is moved to Stage 3. At default, collateral is revalued downward and LGD rises to **45%**.

What is the impairment **before** default, the impairment **after** default, and the P&L charge at the default event?
keyFormulas: Stage 1 ECL = EAD × PD₁₂ₘ × LGD
Stage 3 ECL = EAD × 100% × LGD

working: PD = 100% (default has occurred); LGD revalued to 45%.

intuition: When a loan moves to Stage 3, PD effectively becomes 100% – default is no longer probabilistic, it has happened. The remaining uncertainty is loss-given-default, which is why collateral revaluation drives the post-default provision so heavily.

title: Credit-risk REA – mortgage-heavy retail bank
source: Custom drill on Basel standardised approach
problem:
A retail bank has the following asset mix on its banking-book balance sheet. Compute the **credit-risk REA** under the Basel standardised approach.

| Asset | Value | Risk weight |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cash and central-bank reserves | 50 | 0% |
| Sovereign bonds (AAA) | 200 | 0% |
| Retail mortgages (LTV ≤ 80%) | 600 | 35% |
| Consumer loans | 100 | 75% |
| Corporate loans (unrated) | 50 | 100% |
| **Total assets** | **1,000** | |
keyFormulas: Credit-risk REA = Σ (Asset × Risk Weight)
intuition: A bank with 1,000 of assets carries only 335 of credit-risk REA because most of the book is government exposure (RW=0%) or retail mortgages at the favourable RW=35%. This is why Norwegian and other mortgage-focused savings banks tend to look very well-capitalised on a risk-weighted basis.

title: Credit-risk REA – corporate-focused bank
source: Custom drill on Basel standardised approach
problem:
A wholesale bank has the following asset mix. Compute the **credit-risk REA**.

| Asset | Value | Risk weight |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cash and central-bank reserves | 30 | 0% |
| Sovereign bonds (AAA) | 100 | 0% |
| SME loans | 200 | 75% |
| Investment-grade corporate loans | 300 | 50% |
| Speculative-grade corporate loans | 200 | 150% |
| Equity holdings | 50 | 250% |
| Property, plant & equipment | 20 | 100% |
| **Total** | **900** | |
keyFormulas: Credit-risk REA = Σ (Asset × Risk Weight)
intuition: Compared with the mortgage-heavy bank (REA 335 on 1,000 assets), this corporate bank carries 745 of REA on only 900 of assets. The 150% risk weight on speculative-grade corporates and the 250% weight on equity holdings disproportionately drive REA up – the same balance-sheet size needs ~2× the capital to back.

title: Total REA – credit + market + operational
source: Custom drill on Basel REA composition
problem: A bank's banking-book consists of: 5,000 retail mortgages (RW 35%), 3,000 investment-grade corporate loans (RW 50%), 2,000 speculative-grade corporate loans (RW 150%). Market-risk REA is **100**. Operational-risk REA is **350**. Compute the **total REA**.
keyFormulas: Total REA = credit-risk REA + market-risk REA + operational-risk REA
intuition: Pillar 1 capital requirements (4.5% / 6% / 8%) apply to the **total** REA, not just credit-risk REA. For most commercial banks credit risk dominates (~85–90%), but trading-heavy banks can have material market-risk REA, and even retail banks face operational-risk REA from process, IT and conduct risk.

title: Lilledal Savingsbank – CET1 / T1 / Total capital ratios
source: May 2025 Final, Q6a
problem:
Lilledal Savingsbank balance sheet. Additional REA: **market risk 15**, **operational risk 75**. No own-funds deductions.

**Assets**

| Item | Value | RW |
|---|---:|---:|
| Claims on central bank | 10 | 0% |
| Treasuries | 40 | 0% |
| Retail mortgages | 500 | 35% |
| Loans to corporates | 400 | 100% |
| Other assets | 30 | 100% |
| **Total** | **980** | |

**Liabilities**

| Item | Value |
|---|---:|
| Debt to financial institutions | 30 |
| Retail deposits | 400 |
| Corporate deposits | 120 |
| Senior bonds | 200 |
| Non-preferred senior bonds | 100 |
| Subordinated debt (T2) | 20 |
| Hybrid capital (AT1) | 10 |
| Equity | 100 |
| **Total** | **980** |

Calculate the **CET1 ratio**, **T1 ratio**, and **total capital ratio**.
keyFormulas: Credit-risk REA = Σ (Asset × Risk Weight)
Total REA = credit-risk REA + market-risk REA + operational-risk REA
CET1 ratio  = CET1 ÷ Total REA
T1 ratio    = (CET1 + AT1) ÷ Total REA
Total ratio = (CET1 + AT1 + T2) ÷ Total REA

parts.prompt: Step 3 – own funds (CET1, T1, Total capital).

intuition: All three ratios sit comfortably above the Pillar-1 minimums (4.5% / 6% / 8%). Lilledal is well-capitalised. The favourable 35% risk weight on retail mortgages is why a 980-asset bank carries only 605 of credit-risk REA – most of the book is RW=0% sovereign exposure or RW=35% mortgages, with only 430 in RW=100% claims.

title: Capital ratios for a different capital stack
source: Custom drill on Basel capital tiers
problem:
A bank reports **total REA = 1,000**. Capital structure: equity **90**, AT1 hybrid **15**, T2 subordinated debt **25**.

Compute the **CET1 ratio**, **T1 ratio**, and **total capital ratio**, and compare with the Pillar-1 minimums (4.5% / 6% / 8%).
keyFormulas: CET1 ratio  = CET1 ÷ Total REA
T1 ratio    = (CET1 + AT1) ÷ Total REA
Total ratio = (CET1 + AT1 + T2) ÷ Total REA
intuition: Pillar-1 minimums are the **floor**. Most jurisdictions add a capital-conservation buffer (2.5%), countercyclical buffer (variable), and a systemic-risk / O-SII buffer – pushing the effective minimum CET1 ratio for a typical European bank to ~10–12%. Don't confuse Pillar-1 floors with the **combined buffer requirement**.

title: Reverse-engineering capital from reported ratios
source: Custom drill on Basel capital tiers
problem:
A bank reports CET1 ratio **14.0%**, T1 ratio **15.5%**, total capital ratio **18.0%** on **REA = 800**.

Back out the absolute amounts of **CET1**, **AT1** and **T2** capital.
keyFormulas: CET1 = CET1 ratio × REA
AT1  = (T1 ratio − CET1 ratio) × REA
T2   = (Total ratio − T1 ratio) × REA
intuition: Spreads between ratios = absolute capital in each tier. CET1 ratio + (AT1 capital ÷ REA) = T1 ratio; T1 ratio + (T2 capital ÷ REA) = total ratio. This decomposition is exactly how analysts reverse-engineer a peer bank's capital stack from its disclosure.

title: Lilledal bail-in – required CET1 and waterfall
source: May 2025 Final, Q6c + Q6d
problem:
Continuing from the Lilledal balance sheet (with original capital stack: equity 100, AT1 10, T2 20, non-preferred senior bonds 100, senior bonds 200): the bank has lost most of its equity due to a corporate-loan portfolio collapse and now reports **equity = 20**. Liabilities are otherwise unchanged. Total REA has risen to **700** (driven by stage-3 reclassifications). The resolution authority applies the **bail-in tool** with a target **CET1 ratio of 12%**.

(a) What is the needed CET1 capital to reach the 12% target?
(b) How will it be financed under the bail-in tool? Show the waterfall.
keyFormulas: Required CET1 = target ratio × Total REA
Bail-in waterfall: equity → AT1 → T2 → senior non-preferred → senior unsecured → deposits

working: Non-preferred senior is converted only **partially** (34 of 100) – exactly enough to hit the 12% target. Senior unsecured bonds, deposits and higher-ranked liabilities are **not** touched.

intuition: Bail-in works **bottom-up through the creditor hierarchy** until the target capital ratio is restored. Equity absorbs first, then AT1, T2, senior non-preferred – and crucially, conversion stops at the level where the target is met. Senior unsecured creditors and depositors usually walk away whole, which is precisely what BRRD was designed to achieve: no taxpayer cost, no contagion via senior depositors.

title: Large-bank bail-in – summing the conversion stack
source: Final 2022, Q4 (preserved fragment of grading guide)
problem:
A large bank is recapitalised through bail-in. The resolution authority publishes the following **conversion amounts**:

| Layer | Amount converted to CET1 |
|---|---:|
| Residual shareholders (equity stake retained) | 350 |
| AT1 hybrid capital | 1,000 |
| Subordinated debt (T2) | 1,300 |
| Non-preferred senior bonds | 6,350 |

What is the **total new CET1** after bail-in?
keyFormulas: Total new CET1 = Σ all instruments converted (or retained)
intuition: When the resolution authority publishes conversion amounts, summing them gives total new CET1 directly. The fact that residual shareholders retain 350 – rather than being wiped out – means losses were just barely large enough to require bail-in but did not exhaust pre-existing equity completely.

title: Bail-in waterfall on a richer capital stack
source: Custom drill on BRRD waterfall mechanics
problem:
After loss absorption, a bank reports residual **equity = 5**. Capital and senior structure on the liability side:

| Layer | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Residual equity | 5 |
| AT1 hybrid capital | 25 |
| Subordinated debt (T2) | 40 |
| Non-preferred senior bonds | 80 |
| Senior unsecured bonds | 200 |

The bank's total REA is **1,000**. The resolution authority applies the bail-in tool with a target **CET1 ratio of 10%**.

Compute the required CET1 and walk through the waterfall.
keyFormulas: Required CET1 = target × REA
Conversion order: residual equity → AT1 → T2 → senior non-preferred → senior unsecured (only if necessary)

working: Required CET1 = 100 – target met without touching senior unsecured.

intuition: Bail-in stops the moment the target is met; it does not wipe out everything available. Junior layers are fully converted first because the BRRD waterfall is bottom-up. The remaining un-converted non-preferred senior bonds continue to exist as senior debt of the resolved bank (now better capitalised), and senior unsecured bonds and deposits are entirely untouched.

title: NOK/DKK 6-month FX swap – CIP and swap points
source: May 2024 Final, Q4a (= Final 2022, Q3a)
problem:
Spot price of Danish krone: **S₀ = 1.65 NOK per DKK**. Interest rates: **r_NOK = 4% p.a.**, **r_DKK = 2% p.a.** Tenor: **6 months**.

(i) What is the forward price of DKK in the FX-swap contract?
(ii) Express the price as **swap points**.
keyFormulas: Covered Interest Parity (CIP):  F = S₀ × (1 + r_d × t) / (1 + r_f × t)
where d = home currency (here NOK), f = foreign (DKK), and t = tenor in years
Swap points = F − S₀

working: Swap points = F − S₀ = 1.67 − 1.65 = **0.02 NOK per DKK** = **200 pips**.

intuition: NOK has the higher interest rate, so the forward NOK must **weaken** against DKK to deny arbitrage – the party lending out the higher-yielding NOK has to receive more DKK back at maturity to be compensated. Equivalently, DKK trades at a forward **premium**. This is the core mechanic of CIP.

title: EUR/NOK 1-year FX swap – CIP variant
source: Custom drill on CIP
problem:
Spot rate **S₀ = 11.50 NOK per EUR**. Interest rates: **r_NOK = 4.5% p.a.**, **r_EUR = 3.0% p.a.** Tenor: **1 year**.

Compute the forward rate and the swap points.
keyFormulas: F = S₀ × (1 + r_NOK × t) / (1 + r_EUR × t)
Swap points = F − S₀
intuition: Same mechanic as the NOK/DKK case – the higher-yielding currency (NOK, 4.5%) must depreciate forward against the lower-yielding currency (EUR, 3.0%). The 1.5-pp differential over 1 year produces a ~1.5% forward premium on EUR.

title: Backing out an interest rate from forward and spot
source: Custom drill on CIP – reverse direction
problem:
You observe a 3-month FX-swap quote: **S₀ = 10.50 NOK per EUR** and **F = 10.55 NOK per EUR**. The 3-month EUR rate is **r_EUR = 3.0% p.a.**

What is the **implied 3-month NOK rate** consistent with covered interest parity?
keyFormulas: CIP:  F / S₀ = (1 + r_NOK × t) / (1 + r_EUR × t)
Solve for r_NOK
intuition: If the FX-swap market and money markets are in equilibrium (no arbitrage), CIP holds **identically**. Any persistent deviation (a CIP basis) implies frictions – balance-sheet costs at FX-swap dealers, dollar funding stress, or regulatory constraints. The equation can be inverted in any direction: given any three of {S₀, F, r_d, r_f, t}, solve for the fourth.

title: Miller Manufacturing – moral hazard with equity (Example 7.1)
source: Greenbaum/Thakor/Boot, Contemporary Financial Intermediation, Example 7.1 + Ex Ch7.xlsx (sheet Ex7-1)
problem:
Miller Manufacturing requests a loan of **1.05 M** from your bank. The firm has **1 M of equity** (retained earnings, held as cash) and **2 M of senior debt repayment obligation**. Bank lending is competitive (zero expected profit) and there is no discounting; the bank's loan is junior to the senior debt. Miller can invest the 1.05 M in one of two projects, and the bank cannot directly observe the choice:

| Project | Outcome | Probability |
|---|---:|---:|
| **A** | 2 M / 1 M | 0.8 / 0.2 |
| **B** | 7 M / 0 M | 0.2 / 0.8 |

Miller's existing assets pay 3 M with prob 0.8 and 0 with prob 0.2 (independent of the project).

Assume the bank prices the loan **believing project A will be chosen**. Verify that this is a Nash equilibrium when Miller has the 1 M equity by completing the following four steps.
keyFormulas: Joint distribution of independent random variables
Cash flow available to bank = Total firm cash − senior debt repayment − retained earnings (capped at the repayment obligation P, floored at 0)
Bank zero-profit condition: E[bank receives] = loan principal
Loan rate r = P / loan − 1

parts.prompt: Step 1 – Joint distribution of (Project A + existing assets), with the 1 M equity added.
Step 2 – Cash flow available to service the bank loan after the 2 M senior obligation.
working: If bank requires repayment P, bank actually collects:

parts.prompt: Step 3 – Bank zero-profit condition; solve for the repayment obligation P and the loan interest rate r.
Step 4 – Expected value of equity if Miller does in fact choose project A.
working: (The textbook also computes E[equity | B] = 2.0255 M < 2.150 M, confirming Miller prefers A – so the bank's belief is consistent and we have a Nash equilibrium.)

intuition: Equity is a **commitment device**. With 1 M of skin in the game, Miller's downside under the risky project B is large enough that the safe project A becomes preferred – the bank can therefore price the loan at the safe rate (5.95%). Without the equity (Example 7.1 step 3 of the textbook), the calculation flips: Miller chooses B, the bank anticipates this, and the loan rate jumps. Capital signals **and resolves** moral hazard simultaneously.

title: Borrowers A & B – collateral as a screening device (Example 7.3)
source: Greenbaum/Thakor/Boot, Example 7.3 + Ex Ch7.xlsx (sheet Ex7-3)
problem:
Two borrowers indistinguishable to the bank ex ante:

• **Borrower A (safe):** end-of-period assets = 100 with probability 1.
• **Borrower B (risky):** end-of-period assets = 200 with probability 0.5, 0 with probability 0.5.

Each borrower needs a **30** loan. Riskless rate = **10%**. Everyone is risk-neutral. Collateral worth 1 to a borrower is worth only **0.90** to the bank (10% liquidation haircut).

Design a pair of contracts – secured loan (rate r_s, collateral C) and unsecured loan (rate r_u) – such that A self-selects into the secured contract and B into the unsecured one (Nash separating equilibrium).
keyFormulas: Bank break-even (secured, riskless borrower): 1 + r_s = 1 + r_riskless
Bank break-even (unsecured, default prob 1 − π): [π × (1 + r_u) × L] / (1 + r_riskless) = L
Separating constraint: B's net payoff under unsecured = B's net payoff under secured (B indifferent)

parts.prompt: Step 1 – Interest rate on the secured loan (taken by A, who repays for sure).
working: A repays 30 × (1 + r_s) for sure. Bank break-even discounted at riskless 10%:

parts.prompt: Step 2 – Interest rate on the unsecured loan (taken by B, who repays only in the high state).
working: Repayment probability for B = 0.5. Bank break-even:

parts.prompt: Step 3 – Collateral C that makes B indifferent between the two contracts (so that B does not mimic A).
working: B's expected net payoff under **secured** (loses C in default): 0.5 × (200 − 33) − 0.5 × C = 83.5 − 0.5C.

parts.prompt: Step 4 – Verify A strictly prefers the secured contract (so the equilibrium separates).
parts.answer: A's secured payoff = 67 > A's unsecured payoff = 34
working: A's net payoff under **secured** (collateral surrendered with prob 0): 100 − 33 − 0 × C = 67.
67 > 34 → A strictly prefers the secured contract. **Separating Nash equilibrium confirmed.**

intuition: Collateral works as a **signal** because the risky borrower B has a higher probability of losing it. By demanding C = 33 alongside the low secured rate (10%), the bank makes the secured contract unattractive enough to B that B reveals its type by accepting the 120% unsecured rate instead. Note that the haircut (0.90) does not affect the separating C in this case because the secured loan to A is riskless – A never surrenders collateral in equilibrium.

title: Brown Bakery – collateral against asset substitution (Example 7.4)
source: Greenbaum/Thakor/Boot, Example 7.4 + Ex Ch7.xlsx (sheet Ex7-4)
problem:
Brown Bakery needs a **100** loan. After receiving the loan, Brown chooses between two projects (the bank cannot directly observe which):

• **S (safe):** 300 with probability 0.9, 0 with probability 0.1.
• **R (risky):** 400 with probability 0.6, 0 with probability 0.4.

Riskless rate = **10%**. All parties risk-neutral. Collateral worth 1 to Brown is worth **0.90** to the bank (10% haircut).

Design a contract that induces Brown to choose S and that allows the bank to break even.
keyFormulas: Bank break-even (unsecured, project i with success prob π_i): [π_i × (1+r) × L] / (1+r_f) = L
Bank break-even (secured, success prob π_i, haircut h):
Borrower indifference between projects S and R (with collateral C):

parts.prompt: Step 1 – If the bank offers an unsecured loan priced under the assumption that S will be chosen, show that this is **not** a Nash equilibrium.
parts.answer: r_u^S ≈ 22.22%, but Brown picks R (166.7 > 160.0) – not equilibrium.
working: Brown's expected net payoff under S: 0.9 × (300 − 122.22) ≈ **160.00**.
Brown's expected net payoff under R: 0.6 × (400 − 122.22) ≈ **166.67**.
Brown prefers R → **bank's belief is inconsistent**, no equilibrium.
(The textbook writes 160.2 by rounding the rate to 22% before computing – same qualitative conclusion either way.)

parts.prompt: Step 2 – If the bank instead prices the unsecured loan assuming R, show this is a Nash equilibrium.
parts.answer: r_u^R ≈ 83.33%, Brown picks R (130 > 105) – equilibrium but bad for Brown.
working: Brown's expected net payoff under S: 0.9 × (300 − 183.33) = **105**.
Brown's expected net payoff under R: 0.6 × (400 − 183.33) = **130**.
Brown picks R → consistent with bank's belief → **Nash equilibrium**.

parts.prompt: Step 3 – With a secured loan, find the secured rate r_s and the collateral C that induce Brown to choose S while the bank breaks even.
working: Brown indifference (so Brown does not strictly prefer R):
(The textbook rounds slightly upward to 20.21 for rs and C, to leave the bank with strictly non-negative expected profit after rounding.)

parts.prompt: Step 4 – Verify that the secured contract is a Nash equilibrium and compare Brown's payoff with the unsecured-R equilibrium.
working: Equal by construction (indifference); break the tie in favour of S since the bank also prefers S.

Compared with the unsecured-R equilibrium of 130: Brown is **better off by ~30** under the secured contract, and the bank is indifferent (zero profit either way). Hence the secured contract is the relevant Nash equilibrium under competition.

intuition: Without collateral, Brown chooses R because the loan turns the firm's project-selection problem into a **call-option** problem – Brown captures the upside but the bank absorbs the downside. Collateral attaches a **personal cost to default**, partially restoring the alignment. The cost of imposing collateral is the haircut (0.90 here): a dollar of collateral protection only buys 90 cents of bank recovery, which is why the secured rate (20.20%) is well above the riskless rate (10%) – the bank prices the residual default risk and the haircut into the loan.

title: Diamond-Dybvig: liquidity insurance via two-deposit contracts
source: Ex Ch12.xlsx (sheet 12-2) – Diamond-Dybvig depositor model
problem:
**100 depositors**, each endowed with 1, deposit at the bank at t=0. Each depositor learns at t=1 whether they are an early consumer (D-type, 'diers') or a late consumer (L-type, 'livers'). The probability of being D-type is **0.4**, so 40 D-types and 60 L-types in expectation.

• **D-type utility:**  U_D = √C₁     (wants to consume at t=1 only)
• **L-type utility:**  U_L = 0.6 × √(C₁ + C₂)  (the 0.6 reflects time-discount; cares about total)

The project: invest 1 at t=0 → 1 at t=1 if liquidated, **2.25** at t=2 if held to maturity (1:1 liquidation, 1:2.25 holding).

Compute:

(a) Expected utility under **autarky** (no bank).
(b) The bank's two-deposit contract C₁* = **1.1**, then solve for C₂* under bank break-even.
(c) Expected utility with the bank.
(d) Show that the bank improves welfare.
keyFormulas: Bank break-even (two-deposit contract): 100 − (40 × C₁*) of project rolls at 2.25 to fund 60 L-types' C₂*
Ex-ante expected utility = π_D × √C₁ + π_L × 0.6 × √(C₁ + C₂)

working: D-type alone: liquidate at t=1 → C₁ = 1, C₂ = 0. U_D = √1 = 1.

parts.prompt: (b) Solve for C₂* given C₁* = 1.1 and bank break-even.
working: At t=1 the bank pays 40 D-types × 1.1 = **44** in total.
To pay 44, the bank liquidates 44 of project (1:1).
Remaining 100 − 44 = **56** of project rolls to t=2 at the 2.25 return:

parts.prompt: (c) Expected utility under the bank's two-deposit contract.

working: Mechanism: the bank **pools liquidity risk** across depositors. D-types get 1.1 (better than 1); L-types get 2.1 (worse than 2.25) – but ex ante, before knowing their type, every depositor prefers the contract to autarky.

intuition: This is the core Diamond-Dybvig welfare argument. Without a bank, each depositor must choose **before** learning their type: either liquidate at t=1 (and lose 2.25 if they turn out to be a liver) or hold to t=2 (and consume 0 if they turn out to be a dier). The bank, by writing a contract with state-contingent payouts, converts this all-or-nothing problem into a pooling arrangement. The same intuition motivates **bank-run vulnerability**: the demand-deposit contract (1.1 at t=1) is not backed by enough liquid assets if more than 40 depositors withdraw early, because the project pays 1:1 only on the 56 portion left at t=1 – a self-fulfilling run is possible.
